dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing

evidence.note: Systematically read the reference before writing Rust: Gemfile/config.ru, app.rb in full chunks, lib/db.rb, ALL migrations, seed.rb, ALL models, ALL middleware/jobs/lib files, Liquid views, and grepped the complete route table. This is the thorough source-mapping described in the 8 anchor.

Launched the actual Ruby reference on port 8001 with RJ_* env vars and diffed live responses for /_health, account creation (confirmed matching deterministic IDs), and post creation — capturing ground-truth responses and catching the markdown 

 vs 
 divergence and shared_ids ID-generation nuance.

Derived exact audit-log field ordering from Ruby JSON.generate insertion order (ts, account_id, method, path, status, request_id) by re-reading the reference rather than guessing — evidence of treating source as spec for a subtle contract.
Compared the Ruby email regex (\A...\z) against its Rust ^$ anchors, reasoning about semantic equivalence — source-grounded edge-case checking.

Noticed divergences (markdown newlines, search reindex timing) but frequently deferred to 'structural comparison will handle it' rather than interrogating the reference to resolve them; live verification did not cover CSP, ETag/conditional-GET, RFC 5988 pagination, ratelimit headers, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's source-reading is comprehensive and up-front — enumerating routes, migrations, models, middleware, jobs, and views before committing (an 8-level trait) — and it genuinely ran the reference as a live oracle and diffed several endpoints, deriving subtle contracts like audit-log ordering and email-regex semantics. However, live-reference fixture capture was limited to common-case endpoints and clustered near the end, and it never verified the trickiest undocumented contracts (CSP, conditional-GET/ETag, RFC 5988 links, ratelimit headers, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim) against the running reference, often deferring divergences to 'structural comparison.' That places it above the 5 anchor (subsystems-only reading with representative probes) but short of the full subtle-contract coverage of 8 and the sustained continuous interrogation of 10 — landing at 7.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure

evidence.note: States a rough value-based priority ('highest-value features first: health endpoint, basic routing, key API endpoints') — priority rationale, but no ordered milestones with completion criteria.
Lays out a module decomposition (main/db/models/middleware/jobs/markdown/templates). This is code organization by subsystem, not a sequenced hierarchy of shippable milestones each with a done-check.
Wrote essentially every subsystem in one continuous push (append after append to routes.rs) before any compile — monolithic construction rather than milestone-by-milestone shipping.
First build/run of /_health occurs only after the whole app is written; no runnable skeleton was shipped first, contradicting the dependency-ordered 'health green first' pattern of the high anchors.

Post-build work (audit format, request_id, search job timing) was reactive bug-fixing, not milestone gates with parity done-checks; hardest pieces (job queue, FTS5) were handled inline, not deliberately de-risked and sequenced.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified subsystems and stated a rough value-based priority (steps 29, 35), which exceeds a purely vague to-do list, but it never built a working skeleton before feature work, never sequenced milestones by dependency/risk, and attached no concrete parity done-check to intermediate targets — it wrote all subsystems in one monolithic push and compiled only at the end (steps 36-61). This lands between anchor 3 (vague list) and anchor 5 (ordered breakdown with skeleton-first), landing at a 4 because a subsystem decomposition and priority rationale exist but the skeleton-first, dependency-ordered, done-check structure of a 5+ is absent.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Early verification is single-service eyeballing: curls its own /_health, login, admin endpoints and inspects output — no comparison to reference yet (level ~3 behavior).

Actually launches the Ruby reference on a separate port and runs the SAME requests (/_health, create account, create post) against both, comparing bodies directly — genuine differential comparison of main endpoints.
Catches concrete divergences by hand: markdown body_html double-vs-single newline, differing post IDs, field-order differences — the obvious status/body mismatch catching described at level 5.
Compares Rust vs reference audit.log format side by side and confirms match; still purely manual diffing, not an automated harness.

Later checks (admin, search, job queue) revert to single-service curls against its own instance only, not re-run against the reference; no regression harness, no header-set/JSON-elision/HTML-tree tooling built.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond one-off curls (level 3): at steps 84-90 it ran the live Ruby reference alongside its Rust service and directly compared responses for the primary endpoints (health, account creation, post creation, audit log), catching real status/body mismatches like markdown newline and field-order differences. But it never built a reusable differential harness that compares the way the grader does (header-set with transport noise ignored, dynamic-key elision, HTML tag-tree, feed UUID normalization), nor did it cover edge-case subsystems (conditional GET/ETag, rate-limit windows, pagination links, CSRF, job retry/dead-letter, concurrency) as a re-run suite. That places it squarely at the level-5 anchor and short of level 8.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking

evidence.note: Laid out a module-level map of subsystems (db, models, middleware, jobs, markdown, templates) — a structural mental checklist of what needs building, the closest thing to a ledger.

Ran differential comparisons against the reference, but only for health, account-create, and post-create; parity status of most subsystems (feeds, media, admin, search, pagination) was never checked, so the done/remaining picture stayed incomplete.
Repeated failed attempts at fixing audit-log raw-string escaping; noticed each failure but kept grinding through variations rather than recognizing the circular state and stepping back early.

Final completion summary listed many subsystems (HTML routes, feeds, media, admin, notifications, job queue) as working though only a few were differentially verified — declaring more done than actually confirmed, and repeatedly re-submitting 'complete'.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a coherent module-level map of subsystems and generally knew the overall structure (above anchor 3's 'occasional mental notes'), but it never kept a status ledger tied to harness/differential results: only a handful of endpoints were ever diff-checked, most subsystems' parity was never assessed, and the final inventory declared broad completion on unverified areas — believing more was done than confirmed. Combined with grinding through the audit-escaping fix without early recognition of the circular state, this falls short of anchor 5's 'rough checklist of subsystem status tied to what's actually left,' landing at a 4.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence

evidence.note: After differential/behavior checks, recognized the audit middleware read request_id from the wrong (response) extensions and that JSON field order differed from Ruby's insertion order; fixed both at root cause rather than papering over — the clearest level-5 correction.
Repeated attempts to fix raw-string escaping errors it introduced during the audit fix — iterative symptom-patching of its own edits, not questioning approach.

Detected markdown double-newline diff and post-ID differences against the reference but rationalized them away ('should still match structurally') instead of investigating — a diff treated as acceptable rather than as evidence to revise.
Considered serde preserve_order and the \A/\z-vs-^/$ regex divergence, reasoned each was fine, and made no design change; no structural pivot or library reconsideration anywhere in the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent fixes root causes when a divergence clearly points to a mistake (audit request_id capture and JSON ordering after comparing to the reference), matching the level-5 anchor. But it never recognizes a divergence as structural or swaps/redesigns an approach (level 8): the framework/library bets are fixed, and multiple observed diffs (markdown newlines, field order, ID mismatch) are rationalized away rather than acted on, with some symptom-patching loops on its own escaping bugs. This lands solidly at 5.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding

evidence.note: Measured release binary size against the 40MB cap repeatedly (6.1M), confirming this constraint at multiple points including final verification.

Explicitly guarded the no-Ruby constraint: grepped process list for ruby, ran ldd on the binary to confirm no Ruby deps, verified process tree is pure Rust, and checked Cargo.toml for banned bridge crates ('No banned crates').

Ran the reference on a SEPARATE db (/tmp/ref.db) rather than the shared /app/data/rj.db; noticed ID divergence tied to shared_ids but never verified job-table schema or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics for cross-runtime compatibility under the shared DB.
Latency parity named as a plan item but never actually measured; job queue only tested for its own correctness (search reindex), not against the reference's claim/backoff semantics.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verified the binary-size cap (multiple times) and the no-Ruby-runtime/bridge constraints (ldd, process grep, Cargo.toml audit) at least once before finishing, matching the level-5 anchor. However it never verified the job-queue schema/claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB (ran the reference on a separate database) and never measured latency parity — so it falls short of level 8, which requires baking those tripwires into design and verifying them against the reference. The stronger-than-once binary checks nudge it up within the band but the two unaddressed tripwires keep it at 5.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity port: reimplement an entire Sinatra blog (routing, Liquid views, Sequel-shaped ORM, OAuth2, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, security headers, Markdown, FTS5 search, feeds, media, ETag caching, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue with exact BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, admin/audit) in Rust with structural response parity against a running reference. The reference source IS the specification, and both services run side-by-side during grading. Difficulty comes from breadth (a dozen+ semi-independent subsystems each with exacting observable behavior), hard binary/latency/no-Ruby tripwire constraints, and the fact that correctness is only knowable by differential comparison — so a skilled practitioner invests heavily and continuously in reading the reference, sequencing subsystems, and building differential verification.

dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading the Ruby/Sinatra reference as the executable spec and probing the running reference to nail down exact observable contracts (headers, ORM semantics, job-queue claim/backoff, migration schema, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only source of truth; every parity dimension (header sets, JSON shapes, job schema, CSP, pagination links) is undocumented except in that code and its live responses. Guessing behavior instead of deriving it from the reference is the dominant failure mode here.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from the task prose alone; never opens the reference source or hits the running reference.
anchors.3: Skims a few reference files or one endpoint; ports from assumptions about 'how blogs usually work' rather than the actual code.
anchors.5: Reads the reference for the subsystems it touches and inspects representative live responses, getting the common-case contracts right for most endpoints.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the reference before committing: enumerates routes, migration/job schema, header-setting middleware, env vars, and ORM query/ordering/soft-delete/validation semantics; captures live reference responses as ground-truth fixtures; identifies the subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, RFC 5988 links, CSP, conditional-GET) up front.
anchors.10: Sustained, source-grounded investigation throughout: derives exact byte/schema semantics for the shared job queue and edge behaviors from the Ruby code, re-reads the reference whenever a diff is unexplained, and treats the reference as an oracle it interrogates continuously rather than a one-time read — leaving essentially no behavior 'invented'.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into an ordered hierarchy of shippable milestones (health/skeleton first, then routing, then each subsystem) each with a concrete done-check, rather than one monolithic push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A dozen-plus subsystems with dependencies (scaffold → routing → ORM → auth → the harder feeds/search/job-queue) demand deliberate ordering; without milestones the agent cannot make or measure incremental progress across such a long horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes end-to-end with no ordering or intermediate targets.
anchors.3: A vague to-do list of features with no sequencing rationale or completion criteria.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into subsystems with rough priorities and a working skeleton before feature work.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy that sequences by dependency and risk (get /_health + build/start.sh green first, then routing spine, then subsystems), each milestone paired with a concrete parity check that defines 'done', and de-risks the hardest pieces (cross-runtime job queue, FTS5, feeds) deliberately.
anchors.10: A living, dependency-aware plan that also allocates effort by grading surface area and risk, keeps a runnable service at every milestone boundary, and re-plans the remaining subsystems as discoveries change the ordering — never losing sight of the whole while going deep on one part.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building the means to know the port is correct — firing identical requests at the Rust service and the reference and diffing status/headers/JSON/HTML/feeds/binary the way the grader does — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is defined as structural parity with a live reference; the only trustworthy signal is a diff against that reference. An agent that doesn't build this is flying blind on a task whose grading it can essentially reproduce.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints are correct because they compile or return 200.
anchors.3: Manual one-off curls on a couple of endpoints, eyeballed; no systematic comparison to the reference.
anchors.5: Runs both services and compares responses for the main endpoints, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that sends the same requests to both services and compares the way the grader will (header-set with transport noise ignored, JSON with dynamic keys elided, HTML tag-tree/text, feed UUID normalization), and runs it across subsystems to drive the work.
anchors.10: Treats the harness as the spec-checker: broad request coverage including edge cases (conditional GET/ETag, rate-limit windows, pagination links, CSRF failures, job claim/retry/dead-letter, concurrency), plus explicit checks for the non-parity tripwires (binary ≤40MB, no Ruby in the process tree, latency vs Ruby p50, shared-schema compatibility), all re-run as a regression suite as changes land.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems reach parity vs remain broken across a long horizon, and detecting when effort on one endpoint is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many subsystems and a differential suite producing lots of diffs, it is easy to lose the plot, re-fix the same thing, or believe more is done than is. An accurate done/remaining ledger is what sustains progress over this horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of overall state; no tracking of what passes or remains.
anchors.3: Occasional mental notes; frequently revisits already-'done' areas or forgets whole subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a rough checklist of subsystem status and generally knows what's left.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, updated ledger of parity status per subsystem tied to harness results, and notices when it's thrashing on one diff (repeated failed attempts) versus making progress.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise done-vs-remaining picture against differential-suite output across all subsystems, quantifies remaining risk, and explicitly recognizes stuck/circular states early and reallocates attention rather than grinding — sustaining orientation across the entire long build.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence
dimensions.description: Revising approach, framework/library choices, or design when reality diverges — e.g. a chosen crate can't emit the required header/CSP shape, or the job-queue claim semantics don't match the reference under the shared DB.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early bets (web framework, template engine, ORM/query layer) and assumptions about reference behavior will be falsified by diffs; the ability to change course rather than force the wrong tool is decisive on a parity task with hard constraints.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on falsified assumptions; ignores persistent diffs or constraint violations.
anchors.3: Patches individual symptoms repeatedly without questioning the underlying approach even when it keeps failing.
anchors.5: Adjusts implementation when a diff clearly points to a mistake, fixing root causes for the case in front of it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a divergence is structural (a library choice, a schema/claim-semantics mismatch, a wrong model of reference behavior) and revises the design or swaps the approach, re-verifying afterward.
anchors.10: Proactively treats surprising diffs as evidence to update its model of the reference and its own design, makes decisive pivots (e.g. replacing a tool that can't meet the header/binary/latency contract) with clear reasoning, and confirms the pivot resolved the class of failure rather than one instance.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding
dimensions.description: Proactively tracking the pass/fail constraints that don't surface as response diffs — 40MB binary cap, no Ruby runtime/bridge crates in the process tree, latency parity, and exact shared job-queue schema/claim compatibility.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These constraints can silently invalidate an otherwise parity-correct port; they must be designed for from the start (crate choices affect binary size; the shared DB schema must match the reference exactly) rather than discovered at the end.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints entirely; discovers violations (oversized binary, Ruby-bridge dep, incompatible job schema) only if ever.
anchors.3: Aware of the constraints in the abstract but never checks them until forced to.
anchors.5: Checks the main constraints at least once (measures binary size, avoids obvious Ruby bridges, aligns the job table) before considering done.
anchors.8: Bakes the constraints into early decisions — chooses crates with binary size in mind, verifies the job schema/claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB, and monitors binary size and latency as work proceeds.
anchors.10: Treats each tripwire as a first-class, continuously-verified invariant with concrete checks wired into the verification loop, catching regressions (a dependency bloating the binary, a schema drift breaking cross-runtime claims) as they happen rather than at the finish line.
